THE ONE YOU’VE ALL BEEN WAITING FOR: COLLAGEN CHAT (Girl Science Edition) 🩷 First up, collagen is important. It’s what keeps your skin bouncy, joints cushioned, and tissues strong. Your body makes collagen, but rom your mid-20s, that production starts to dip – and drops faster post-menopause thanks to hormonal changes. DO YOU NEED TO TAKE A COLLAGEN SUPPLEMENT? Collagen supplements don’t “top up” your collagen directly. They’re broken down into small peptides that signal your body to make more, but only if your body’s in the right state to respond. That generally comes from you sleeping well, eating a balanced diet with enough protein and managing your stress, Without those foundations, the signal’s weak – and your collagen powder probably won’t do much. Where collagen actually delivers: 💞Joints: Hydrolysed or type II collagen can help reduce joint pain and slow cartilage breakdown (especially if osteoarthritis runs in your family). 🌟Skin: Evidence is mixed. High-quality, independent studies show minimal benefit for elasticity or hydration. 💅Hair & nails: Not much science here yet. Takehome message: collagen can support you, but it’s not a miracle. Focus on your foundations first – balanced nutrition, sleep, and stress management – and collagen becomes the cherry on top, not the whole sundae 🍒 #collagen #collagenforwomen #girlscience #womenshealth #hormonehealth

Does collagen actually make your skin look younger? 🧬 Collagen supplements are everywhere - powders, capsules and drinks promising better hydration, elasticity and fewer wrinkles. But when researchers actually looked at the evidence, things got interesting. A 2026 systematic review looked at 25 randomised controlled trials. Most reported improvements in hydration, elasticity or wrinkles. Sounds convincing, right? But the majority of those trials were judged to have a high risk of bias. And a 2025 meta-analysis of 23 RCTs found something even more interesting: when researchers looked specifically at higher-quality studies, the apparent benefits disappeared. That doesn't prove collagen supplements don't work. It means the evidence is much less definitive than the marketing would have you believe. There may well be a benefit — but we still need better-quality, larger and longer-term trials to know how meaningful that benefit actually is. Study the evidence. Not the marketing. #collagenpeptides #Collagen #SkinHealth #Aesthetics

🐟 Your collagen TYPE is only part of the story. Type I. Type II. Type III. Type IV. Type V. Collagen brands have gotten very good at putting multiple collagen types on the front of a bottle and making us believe that more types automatically means a better collagen. But when I vet a collagen supplement, I want to know something else: Where did that collagen actually come from, and how was it processed? Collagen is animal-derived. Bovine means cow. Marine means fish. And if you are consuming an animal derived ingredient every single day, I believe the source and manufacturing process deserve just as much attention as the Roman numeral on the label. A 2022 scientific review titled Collagen Extraction from Animal Skin examined methods used to extract collagen from animal hides. The cattle section is particularly interesting. Published bovine hide extraction protocols described in the review include: • Lime treatment for dehairing • 2% sodium hydroxide (NaOH) treatment for 5 days • Sulfide solution for hair removal • Acetone treatment repeated 5 to 7 times in one protocol • 0.5 M sodium hydroxide for hair removal for 24 hours in another • 10% butyl alcohol for fat removal • Hydrochloric acid (HCl) • Acetic acid extraction • A lime treatment containing sodium sulfide (Na₂S) and calcium oxide (CaO) followed by deliming with ammonium chloride and concentrated HCl in another protocol. And this isn't simply a cattle issue. The review explains that conventional collagen extraction has typically relied on chemical hydrolysis using acids, alkalis or salt solubilization. It lists sodium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide among alkaline pretreatments and notes that NaOH pretreatment can last from a few days to weeks. For acid extraction, the authors list acetic, chloroacetic, citric, and lactic acids, as well as hydrochloric, sulfuric, and nitric acids. Now, an important distinction: The presence of these chemicals during manufacturing does not prove that harmful amounts remain in the finished collagen supplement. Collagen goes through additional isolation and purification steps, including processes such as precipitation, centrifugation, dialysis, and filtration. My point is not: “Chemical used = toxic collagen.” My point is: Why are we choosing collagen based almost entirely on Type I vs II vs III while asking so few questions about the raw material and how it was processed? The researchers themselves note that processing conditions, including pretreatment, can influence characteristics and quality of the extracted collagen. And there's another misconception worth clearing up. Type I collagen is the predominant fibrillar collagen in many tissues and is present in the connective tissues of the skin and bone. Type III is also present in skin. So simply putting five collagen types into a supplement does not establish that it is a better product for your skin. For my own daily supplement, I prefer a traceable, wild-caught marine source, predominantly Type I, in hydrolyzed peptide form. But even the word “marine” isn't enough for me. I still want to know the species, sourcing, dose, processing, and contaminant testing. That is also why I pay attention to the word peptides. Hydrolyzed collagen has been broken into smaller peptide fragments. It doesn't mean Type I collagen travels intact from your stomach into your face. Your body digests and utilizes those building blocks. So when you're comparing collagen supplements, stop at the back of the bottle and ask: SOURCE → TISSUE → PROCESSING → DOSE → TESTING Not just: TYPE I → II → III → IV → V That is the difference between reading the marketing and actually vetting the raw material.
